interviewQuestions.question: What actually happens when an LLM "generates" the next word?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd walk through it as a pipeline, not magic: the prompt gets tokenized into subword tokens, each token is embedded and passed through stacked decoder blocks (masked self-attention + feedforward, with residuals and normalization), and the final layer produces a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for "what comes next."

A decoding strategy (greedy, or sampling with temperature/top-p) then picks one token from that distribution, appends it to the sequence, and the whole forward pass repeats — one token at a time, autoregressively, using a KV cache so it doesn't redo attention over tokens it already processed. There's no separate "thinking" step; the fluency and reasoning we see is what emerges from repeating "predict the most plausible next token" long enough, at large enough scale, over enough data.

**Testing:** whether you understand that generation is repeated next-token sampling, not a single holistic act, and that you know where tokenization, attention, and decoding each fit in.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: How next-token generation actually works

interviewQuestions.question: Why does doubling an LLM's context window cost more than twice as much compute, and what makes long-context requests expensive in practice?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Self-attention computes a relationship between every pair of tokens in the sequence — each token attends to every other token — so the amount of work scales with the square of the sequence length, not linearly. Double the context length and you don't get twice the attention computation, you get roughly four times as much, because there are now roughly four times as many token pairs to compute attention scores between. This quadratic scaling is a structural property of the attention mechanism itself, not an implementation inefficiency someone forgot to fix.

In practice this shows up as both compute cost and memory cost. The **KV cache** — the cached key/value vectors for every previous token, kept around so each new token doesn't have to recompute attention over the whole history — grows linearly with context length, and at long context lengths (tens of thousands of tokens) that cache alone can become the dominant memory consumer on the serving GPU, sometimes larger than the model's own weights. That's why providers charge more per token for longer contexts and why serving infrastructure specifically optimizes KV cache management (eviction, compression, paging) as a first-class concern rather than an afterthought.

The practical engineering response isn't just "use a bigger GPU" — techniques like sliding-window attention, or retrieval-augmented approaches that keep the actual context shorter by fetching only relevant chunks, exist specifically to avoid paying the quadratic cost when the full context isn't genuinely needed for every token.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the quadratic cost from the attention mechanism itself, and connect it to the concrete KV-cache memory consequence in serving.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why long context is expensive

interviewQuestions.question: Your team is deciding between training a smaller model on more data versus a larger model on less data, for a fixed compute budget. How do you reason about that trade-off?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is exactly the question Chinchilla-style scaling-law research answered empirically: for a fixed compute budget, there's a specific optimal ratio between model size and training data, and many earlier large models were actually under-trained relative to their parameter count — they'd have performed better as a smaller model trained on proportionally more tokens for the same compute spend, rather than a bigger model that never saw enough data to use its capacity well.

My approach would be to treat this as an empirical question, not a guess: fit a scaling curve using several smaller, cheaper training runs at different model-size/data-size combinations, extrapolate where the loss-vs-compute curve is minimized for the target compute budget, then commit the full budget to that configuration rather than picking a size based on intuition or what's fashionable. This is standard practice precisely because getting it wrong wastes a very expensive training run.

Beyond the pure loss-minimization answer, I'd weigh two more practical factors: a smaller model is cheaper and faster to serve at inference time for the entire product lifetime, which usually dwarfs the one-time training cost — so if the scaling curve shows a smaller model at a proportionally larger data budget performs comparably, that's often the better overall choice even beyond what the training-compute-optimal point alone suggests. I'd also check whether enough high-quality training data actually exists to feed a larger token budget — the ideal ratio from the scaling law assumes data isn't the bottleneck, which increasingly it is for very large runs.

**Testing:** whether you know scaling laws give a real answer to this trade-off, not just an intuition, and that you'd factor in serving cost, not only training-time loss.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Model size vs data size under a fixed compute budget
